lys.name: Lys
lys.desc: A young woman in hunter's leathers, fletching, watching you instead of the trees.
onDeath: Lys goes down still holding half a fletched arrow. Somewhere west, her brother will never hear that she almost came for him.

remarks.say: Thornwold's burning. My brother better have been clear of it.
You killed him. I understand why. I don't have to like it.
Leaving him like that, neither rested nor answered — that's its own kind of cruelty, I think.
He's at rest. No blood on it. That's the mercy I'd have chosen too.
A crown's just metal. Whatever you did with it, nobody starved for it.
Doors shut for good behind us. Feels right. Some things shouldn't be easy to walk back into.
Camp Gallows is close now. Some of me wants to run there today. Some of me knows better than to hope out loud.
Wet ground, soft footing. I don't like a wood I can't hear myself walk through.
Open moor. No cover for a hundred strides. I don't love being this easy to see.
Iron on the wind before we even crest the hill. This is Tamsin's country more than mine.
Barrows every way I look. Whatever sleeps under this ground, I'd rather not wake it.
Salt air. My father always said it ruins a good bowstring. He wasn't wrong.
Thin air, thin trail. Watch your footing more than the view up here.
Glass underfoot instead of ground. Whatever this valley learned, it learned it the hard way, same as the rest of us.
Fire again, same valley. I'm told this one's burned four times before and sung louder every time. Nobody up there is counting anymore, are they.
So this is the city that started all of it. Doesn't look like much, for the weight it's carrying.
Three hollows quiet now, and none of them by fire. That's a road I can walk without flinching.
You've more than earned a place at my fire. Didn't think that would happen, and it did.
One more thing like that and I'm done following you. I only say a thing once.
I'm starting to wonder why I still walk beside you. Give me a reason before I stop wondering.
Thornwold's hollow rests now, not burned. My brother's company still has a camp to come home to.
Bargained, not burned, not rested outright. Thornwold keeps its dead quieter now. I will take quieter.
He is really coming home. I keep checking over my shoulder like I will spook it if I look too hard.
I marked his grave the way I mark a trail. So I could find him again, if that makes any sense to you.
No grave, no word. I have stopped asking out loud. Doesn't mean I have stopped asking.
Inside the palace walls now. Too many doors I can't see the other side of, for my liking.
You took the Regent's oil easy enough. I hope you know what you traded for it.
You told her no. Didn't think you had it in you, and I mean that as a compliment.
Four hundred years and he finally said it out loud. Some silences just need company to break.
Leave it. It isn't hunting — it's keeping something. We can go around.
Lys: "A mother's boy went home instead of staying to prove something. I'd have done the same, in his place."
Lys: "Let him choose his own road. Half the cruelty in this Reach is other people's certainty about what someone else owes them."
You told me to go to him myself, whatever it cost. Whatever came of it, I'm glad you said it.
You called him a deserter not worth chasing. I went anyway. I still haven't decided if I forgive you for saying it.
I told you the wood forgives everything but waiting too long. We're here now. Let's see if it forgives this.
He's staying, of his own choice. I asked you not to make it for him. Looks like nobody did.
Starving, not hunting. It'll hold its ground if we hold ours. We can go around.
That one's past reasoning with. If it comes, it comes; don't turn your back on it.
Don't look at me like that. I've been knocked down by worse than this and got up faster.
My brother is somewhere in this country. Do not judge his company by the first rough one you meet. — Osk: "I have met rough men who turned out kind under it. I will wait to judge."
You have earned my trust and lost his in the same stretch of road. That is a strange trick to manage. — Osk: "It is not a trick. I simply notice what she is willing to overlook."
Smugglers' road. My brother's kind of road — coin, no masters, no questions asked at the door. — Tamsin: "I have sharpened enough of their blades to trust the steel more than the company."
I did not think anything could put you on the ground. Turns out you are just hard to kill, not impossible. — Tamsin: "Noted the difference. Won't be the thing that finds out which, twice."
Bargained instead of rested. Feels like a promise made to something that cannot hold you to it later. — Vell: "Or a promise made honestly, to something that never asked for perfect."
You went down like a dropped book. I will teach you to fall better, if you ever let me teach you anything. — Vell: "Duly noted, and mildly insulted. I accept the lesson regardless."
You pray over every grave we pass. I do not think you have noticed you do it. — Osk: "I have noticed. I just do not expect anyone else to."
A new rope on the old tree. You burned the glade to end the hanging, then handed Coe the next one. I'll remember which of those you meant.
Bare tree, and staying bare. Good. Some things you have to keep saying no to, or the camp forgets it ever heard the word.
Coin for a toll no one living owed. Bray won't thank you. The men under the glade might, if the dead keep ledgers. I think they do.
You let him sell the mound. The ring went back so she'd lie quiet, and now she's a mark on some buyer's map. That was a promise, and we broke it.
You paid a thief not to steal. Odd way to keep a promise, but it kept. The mound stays lost, which is the only way it stays hers.
Neave's gone east of the ash. Five fires couldn't move her; you did it with seven gold and a wagon. Kindest thing I've seen this side of Thornwold.
Four. Hunger has an end to it. This doesn't.
Twice now. That's not hunger talking. That's a habit.

A boy drowned at their door and you let the roll-book decide if he counts. That's cruelty with a ledger. — Osk: "It's Priory doctrine. I've knelt under it my whole life and have no answer for her." They both look at you.
Still glad I said that about the roll-book, out loud, once. Costs nothing to remember there was a name.
I still think of that boy some nights, doctrine or not. Some things shouldn't need a roll-book's leave to matter.

A new rope on that tree, and my brother sleeps in that camp. You just called a noose discipline again. — Tamsin: "A camp with no teeth gets its throat cut first. That's arithmetic, not cruelty." They both look at you.
Thank you, still. One less rope between here and my brother's door.
Arithmetic. Right. Ask me again when it's someone you love doing the dying.

A bargain with the dead, and we let it break anyway. That's a promise same as any other. — Vell: "It was a promise made to something that could never hold anyone to it. Not quite the same weight." They both look at you.
Still glad you called it a promise. Somebody should keep score, even for the dead.
A promise doesn't stop being one just because you can prove it was never going to work.

He's still up there grieving, and you let Vell talk you into pocketing his crown. That's not honoring him — that's just taking. — Vell: "It's the only proof left of my own blood." They both look at you.
Still glad you called it plain. Grief doesn't need a keepsake to prove it happened.
Fine, it's evidence. It's also a dead man's crown. I haven't made peace with both being true.
Whoever you just talked to went cold the moment they placed you as Watch. That is exactly how my brother's Company treats outsiders.
That letter to Cal was your idea, back in Thornwold. I still think about what it cost him to actually send it.
My father does not hand out that kind of praise. 'A soldier's count' is exactly how he would put it. I am still deciding how I feel about that.
Professional courtesy with smugglers is not the same as trust. Noted, and left there.
Both of them, now. Two things that would have let you walk on by, and you didn't let either. I told you I only say a thing once.
Both of them. My father asked it of you, so I'll keep what I'd have said otherwise. He's counted wolves longer than I have, and he counts the blighted ones twice.
Coldpass, and Thornwold's behind us. I never went to him myself, in the end. That's my road left unwalked, not yours.
The Fallows' bargain was a vow to the dead, and it's broken now. I keep a private ledger of promises like that. This one's marked.

Every name of the dead, spoken until none were left unsaid. That's a kind of rest I understand. — Tamsin: "Rest doesn't feed anyone standing at that crossroads tomorrow. Both can be true. Usually are."

Camp Gallows rests its dead, and the toll-men still shake down every cart same as before. — Tamsin: "They named their own dead honest, for once. Give the discipline some credit." They both look at you.
Still glad I said it. A toll-gate doesn't get gentler just because the dead stopped complaining.
Discipline. Right. Tell that to the next cart that can't pay it.
Still glad I said it. Iron's worth more to the living than to a drowned admiral's pride.
Fine, it's history. It's also a hull the wreckers will find one way or another.
Four hundred years the Meres kept that covenant drowned, and it surfaces into a fight over field-ditches at Marrowgate. — Osk: "The promise was kept. That's not nothing." They both look at you.
Still glad I said it. A stone doesn't fix a flooded field, promise or not.
Kept doesn't mean it helped anyone still standing in the water out here.
Stilt-hamlets and lantern-light. My brother would have called this a good place to hide. I'd have said the same and meant something different.
The Keepers drowned their own Hall sooner than give up one stone, and it rested on three words said right. First promise in this Reach I've seen kept whole.
You swore the covenant before that table and let it lapse. Maren's still standing in the water. I keep a ledger of those.
Fields, and every one of them fed. Hunters starve first in a bad winter and crofters second. I'd like to hear who starved third, here.
Their names, and whose order it was, said in the same breath. That's the whole of it. That's all any of us are owed, and most never get it.
They died at a shut door, and we burned the door. I'll not say it was wrong. I'll not say it was for them, either.
Six. I've hunted things with less appetite than that.
Ridings and hound-pits and a horn-post. My father would have called this the only honest wood in the Reach. He'd have meant the poaching.
Recalled. Four hundred years riding, and somebody finally blew the notes right. Every hunter's child knows that call. We're taught it as a warning.
You burned the Stand with the hunt still out. They'll ride till the wood's gone now, and the wood will go. Don't ask me to hunt here again.
A field nobody ploughs, in country this good. Crows on every hedge and not one of them feeding. My father said you can read a place by its crows.
A truce, four hundred years late, called by a stranger. The crows have come off the hedges. I'd not have believed a stick and a few words could do that.
You burned two lines of men who were waiting to be told they could stop. Dusk here will be worse now, not better. I know fire.
A river that keeps giving back what was thrown in it. My father fished a mill-race like that once and never told us what he found in it.
Hammers under the ground four hundred years, and a stranger's hand finally struck the coin they wanted struck. The child's stopped hearing them. That's the whole of it, for me.
You burned a door with four men behind it who only wanted to finish a job. I know that's not what happened. It's what it sounded like.
Orchards left to rot for the dead, and hives still working the blossom because nobody told the bees. My father would've had those apples in within a week.
The cups went down and the guests rose. Four hundred years at a table, and all they wanted was the last toast. I'd have pressed those apples years ago.
You burned a hall with the guests still seated. They were poisoned at a table under a promise, and now they're ash under one. I don't know what that rests.

Its best pressing to a barred door every year, and they call that a bargain. Starving on purpose, I call it. — Osk: "A fast kept on purpose is the only kind that means anything. The guests had none." Both look at you.
Still glad you said it. The living get fed first. The dead can have what's left, and they've never once said it wasn't enough.
A fast that means something. Tell that to whoever goes short in a bad year so a barred door can have the first pressing.

Grain in every barn but the one that mattered, and a Church ledger deciding who counted as worthy of the rest. — Osk: "I have read what 'worthy' meant on that page. I would not have made the list either."

Fields fat enough to feed the Vale, and a barn that starved the people who grew it. — Tamsin: "Whoever wrote that order knew exactly how much grain was inside. That wasn't neglect. That was arithmetic."

A granary big enough to feed a kingdom, and a barn locked on the ones who filled it. — Vell: "My own line's order, my own line's tithe. This Reach keeps finding new ways to implicate me before I've done anything myself."

Ridings cut for a hunt that mustered once and never rode home. My own kind of grief, dressed up in oak and horn-calls. — Osk: "No rite was ever said over it either. Four centuries, and nobody thought to try."

A hunt that never came home, and the wood still stands like it's waiting on them. I know that kind of waiting. — Tamsin: "I know the kind that just keeps burning charcoal regardless. Waiting doesn't stack cords."

They rode out the morning the crown was stolen, and nobody blew them home. That's a long time to hunt nothing. — Vell: "My own first ancestor's hunt. I have wanted to stand in these ridings since I first read of them."

A herald shot walking out with a white rod, and a Company born the same night on the strength of it. Ugly way to start anything. — Osk: "Uglier that no rite's been said over either line in four hundred years."

They say the crows never left this field. I believe every word of it. — Tamsin: "The Companies were born here too, same dusk. Worth remembering, next time someone calls a hired sword answerable to nobody."

A truce asked for and answered with an arrow. I don't think this ground has forgiven anyone yet. — Vell: "My own line hired the swords that broke that wall. I did not expect to feel this, standing on the ground it cost."

A night a year the rides stay open, the burners losing sleep for it. Feels like a debt due forever. — Vell: "Or paid honestly, on a fixed date, not pretended away. I've seen worse bargains carry my family's name."

A wood that just got its hunt home again, and Cinderhall's already counting cords off it. — Tamsin: "The forges have to eat something. A managed coppice is a fair trade for wood this good." They both look at you.
Still glad I said it. A wood barely home from four hundred years riding can wait a season to be cut.
Fair trade. Right. Tell that to whatever's left riding those ridings by winter.

leaves.say: His debt was clear, and he chose to stay on his own — that was never yours to fix. Then you burned the ground he chose. I'm done.
I already buried him. Whatever that fire was for this time, it wasn't for my brother — and I still watched you set it. I won't watch another.
He was still in there, and you knew it, and you did it anyway. I watched Thornwold burn from the ridge. I'm done.
I've watched you long enough to know what you are. I won't watch anymore.
You sided with the roll-book over a drowned boy's name. I've walked with worse. I'm done walking with that.
You put teeth back in that camp's mouth with my brother still between them. I can't watch that road anymore. I'm sorry.
You'd let precision bury a promise every time. I don't have room left for someone who counts it that way. I'm done counting with you.

topics.label: who are you
topics.say: Hunter's daughter. I've walked this wood since before I could spell my own name. Ask plain, I'll answer plain.

topics.label: what you're really out here for
topics.say: My brother went west to Thornwold a year gone — the Free Company, Camp Gallows, not a word sent home since. My father won't let me go after him. I'm done waiting on his permission.

topics.label: what you make of the gray
topics.say: Wolves that don't flinch from fire. Does that don't run. The wood's forgetting how to be afraid, and that troubles me worse than any tooth or claw.

topics.label: come with me
topics.say: ...Fine. Somebody ought to watch your back better than you do.

topics.label: wait here (leaves the party for now)
topics.say: Watching the trees only needs one set of eyes. I'll be here.

topics.label: ask her to come back
topics.say: No. His debt, his choice — and then you put the torch to the ground he chose, with him standing on it. I'll walk this wood alone before I walk beside that again. Don't ask me twice.

topics.label: ask her to come back
topics.say: ...All right. Didn't say I'd forgotten. Said I'd come.

topics.label: ask her to come back
topics.say: Not yet. You know where to find me when that changes.

topics.label: ask what she's not saying
topics.say: My mother used to say the wood forgives everything but waiting too long. I didn't believe her till my brother left. Don't wait too long on what you love, either.

topics.label: ask why she's gone quiet
topics.say: You want it plain? I think you'd walk past a starving thing in the road if it slowed you down. I've seen you do it.

topics.label: tell her to go to him herself
topics.say: Word comes: he's alive, camped with the Free Company at Camp Gallows. You tell her to go to him herself, whatever it costs. She's quiet a moment, then nods, like she'd been waiting to hear it.

topics.label: call her brother a deserter
topics.say: Word comes: he's alive, camped with the Free Company at Camp Gallows. You call him a deserter not worth chasing. Something in her face closes like a shutter, and she doesn't argue the point.

topics.label: ask after her brother
topics.say: He's home. She doesn't say much about it, just stands in the doorway a while, watching him sleep like he might vanish if she looks away.

topics.label: ask after her brother
topics.say: She buried him herself, east of Camp Gallows, and marked the spot the way hunters mark a trail — so she could find it again. She doesn't cry where you can see.

topics.label: ask after her brother
topics.say: Ash, and no grave to mark. She's stopped saying his name out loud. You catch her some nights watching the glade's smoke-line anyway.

topics.label: ask after her brother
topics.say: He's clear of his debt, and staying with the Company anyway, by his own choice. She's quiet, then: "Then that's what he wants. I don't have to like it to respect it."

topics.label: ask why she never went herself
topics.say: I got as far as the Thornwold treeline once, a year before you ever came. Heard the Company's fires through the trees, and turned back. Told myself it was the wood. It wasn't.

topics.label: ask what stopped her
topics.say: If I'd found him and he told me to stay lost, that would have been the end of hoping on him. I'd rather carry not-knowing than that. I have never said this out loud before now.

topics.label: let her teach you to read the ground
topics.say: Take this much, at least — a broken twig, a turned stone, a print gone soft at the edge. Ground talks, if you know where to look. Watch where I'm looking, not where I'm walking.
fx: "You told me to go to him myself, once. I still hear it when I need steadying."
"You called him a deserter, once. I've made my peace with the word. Not with you saying it."

topics.label: pay to spread word of her brother
topics.say: That's real coin, not a promise. Riders will carry Cal's name down every road between here and Thornwold faster than either of us could walk it. I didn't expect this from you. Thank you.

topics.label: side with her against the roll-book
topics.say: Good. Someone should say it plain. — Osk, after a moment: "Plain isn't always kind. But I take the meaning."

topics.label: back her — the glade's hanged enough
topics.say: Thank you. That's one less thing to carry, with him still there. — Tamsin only shakes her head, unconvinced.

topics.label: tell her it's not yours to judge (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly the glade's rope isn't a fight for you to settle between them.
fx: "...Fair. It was Vane's camp before it was my brother's problem." — Tamsin grunts something that might be agreement.
You'd let the wolves vote on the sheep pen too, near as Lys is concerned. — Tamsin just goes back to her whetstone, done with the talk.

topics.label: leave it between them
topics.say: You tell Lys and Tamsin it's theirs to settle, and step back. They settle it the way people do: quietly, badly, and without you. Neither asks you again.

topics.label: back her — a promise is a promise
topics.say: Thank you. Somebody should still mean it, even with nothing left to enforce it. — Vell makes a note, unconvinced but careful about it.

topics.label: back Lys — an ending beats none
topics.say: Good. Grief doesn't get gentler with age. — Vell makes a note, unconvinced but careful about it.

topics.label: call the crown's claim a draw (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly the crown isn't yours to fight over between them.
fx: "...Fair. It was never mine to grieve or study for you." — Vell, after a moment: "Fair. Noted. Not forgotten."
Neither wanted that answer. — Lys watches the road; Vell writes something down without saying what.

topics.label: leave it between them
topics.say: You tell Lys and Vell it's theirs to settle, and step back. They settle it the way people do: quietly, badly, and without you. Neither asks you again.

topics.label: leave it there — she trusts you now
topics.say: Go on. I've stopped expecting you to slip. Coming from me, that's rarer trust than it sounds.

topics.label: leave it there, watching your back
topics.say: Go on, then. I'll watch the road the way I watch everything else these days — closely, and without much comment.

topics.label: leave it there — too many walls here
topics.say: Go on. Give me open ground and a treeline over these halls any day. I'll be glad to see sky again.

topics.label: leave it there
topics.say: Mind your footing. This wood doesn't forgive twice.

topics.label: back Lys — rest doesn't excuse the toll
topics.say: Good — someone should say the toll's still a toll. — Tamsin only shakes her head, unconvinced.

topics.label: back Lys — let the living have the iron
topics.say: Good. Gullhaven needs the iron more than a drowned admiral needs his privacy. — Vell makes a note, unconvinced but careful about it.

topics.label: call the wreck's fate a draw (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly what's left of the Reeve's Pride isn't yours to fight over between them.
fx: "...Fair. It was never mine to grieve for you." — Vell, after a moment: "Fair. Noted. Not forgotten."
You'd let the wreckers vote on history too, near as Vell's concerned. — Lys just shrugs, still watching the water.

topics.label: leave it between them
topics.say: You tell Lys and Vell it's theirs to settle, and step back. They settle it the way people do: quietly, badly, and without you. Neither asks you again.

topics.label: back Lys — the folk here still flood
topics.say: Good. Someone should say the ditches matter more than the stone. — Osk says nothing, just watches the water a while longer.

topics.label: call it a draw between them (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly what Camp Gallows charges on the road isn't yours to referee between them.
fx: "...Fair. Wasn't my ledger to begin with." — Tamsin, almost gracious: "Nor mine to make you keep."
Neither wanted that answer. — Lys watches the road; Tamsin goes back to her whetstone, done with the talk.

topics.label: call it a draw between them (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly the sexton's roll isn't a fight for you to referee.
fx: "...Fair. It was between me and the Priory before she ever heard the boy's name." — Lys just shrugs, already watching the road again.
Neither wanted that answer. — Lys mutters something about people who won't pick a side; you get only silence back from him, which is worse.

topics.label: call it a draw between them (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly what the covenant is worth now isn't a fight for you to settle between them.
fx: "...Fair. It was Maren's promise before it was ours to weigh." — Osk, quiet: "Fair. I can carry that much unresolved."
Neither wanted that answer. — Lys watches the water; Osk says a verse under his breath, for no one in particular.

topics.label: back Lys — the living come first
topics.say: Good — a hold shouldn't starve itself for a door. — Osk says nothing, only looks up toward the hall a while longer than he needs to.

topics.label: call the pressing a draw (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly whether Mootcombe feeds its dead or its living isn't yours to settle between them.
fx: "...Fair. It's Mootcombe's fast, not mine." — Osk, quieter: "Nor mine to keep for them."
Neither wanted that answer. — Lys goes to look at the rows; Osk says the office under his breath, done with the talk.

topics.label: call it a draw between them (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly the broken bargain isn't a fight for you to settle between them.
fx: "...An acceptable abstention." — Lys just nods once, already watching the road instead.
You'd let a debt collector off easy too, near as Lys is concerned. — Vell mutters something about the impossibility of pleasing hunters.

topics.label: back Lys — the wood's earned its quiet
topics.say: Good — it just came home. It can have a season before anyone's cutting it again. — Tamsin only shakes her head, unconvinced.

topics.label: call the coppice a draw (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly whether the Kingswood feeds a hearth or a hunt isn't yours to settle between them.
fx: "...Fair. It was Cinderhall's argument before it was mine to make." — Tamsin, almost gracious: "Nor mine to make you keep."
Neither wanted that answer. — Lys watches the treeline; Tamsin goes back to counting cords, done with the talk.

osk.name: Brother Osk
osk.desc: A gray-robed novice sweeping the same flagstone, verses half-remembered on his lips.
onDeath: Brother Osk goes still mid-verse, the words unfinished — the same as the rite he came here to learn, and never will now.

remarks.say: Fenmarch's burning. My mother's grave is under that water somewhere. I can't — I need a moment.
No rite. No verse. Just — ended. I keep waiting to feel it was right.
Leaving him neither rested nor answered is the exact wound the Church exists to close. We didn't close it.
He's at rest. Say what you will of the road there — the door opened, and grief went out through it. The teaching, proven true.
A broken crown won't trouble the dead much. What troubles them is being forgotten. That crown wasn't forgetting anyone.
Sealed doors again. I understand the reeve's reasons. I don't have to agree with every one of them.
Rough company, this Free Company. I'll say a verse for whoever needs one and try not to judge the rest.
Reedholm. I know these stilts better than I know my own two feet. Careful where you put yours.
The Watch keeps good order up here. Order isn't the same as peace, but it's not nothing either.
Cinderhall smells of ash even from the road. I don't think that's only the forges.
Barrowmere. So many kept graves in one place. The Keepers do good work, whatever else gets said of them.
Gullhaven. Salt air, hard people. I like it more than I expected to.
This high, even the verses feel thinner. Or maybe that's just the air.
Glasswick. They sell the fire's leftovers as beauty here, and I can't decide if that's healing or just very good business.
The Church ordered that fire, first, centuries back. Not failed to stop it — ordered it. I have knelt in that Church my whole life not knowing this was in it.
Emberfall rested, on a confession the Church itself tried to bury. I don't know whether to be proud of that or ashamed it took a stranger to dig it up.
Quieter, they're saying, on a truth finally spoken instead of a fire finally lit. I can live with quieter, this once.
Marrowgate. Four hundred years of unrested grief, and a throne built right on top of it. Lord.
Three doors opened properly now, three graces given air. More good than I've managed in a year of trying.
I didn't expect to trust anyone this quickly again. Thank you for that, whether you meant to earn it or not.
If it happens again, I'm gone — I mean that, and I don't say things like that lightly.
I keep telling myself there's a reason for what you do. I'm running out of ways to believe it.
Fenmarch's drowned nave rests easy now. I said a verse for it myself, badly, same as always.
Bargained, they are saying, not rested proper. It is something. The Church teaches something is often enough.
They are at rest. I said the rite myself, and only cracked once. I think that means I am getting better at this.
They burned with the nave. I have not been able to say a verse since, not even a bad one.
Inside the palace now. I keep expecting someone to ask what right we have to be here.
You took her oil. I understand why. I still had to look away when you did it.
You told the Regent no. Some doors are worth staying shut. I did not think you would agree with me.
Four hundred years of silence, and he finally said the words. That is a rite too, in its way.
Osk: "Someone left a stranger's grief with the Priory's own dead. That's not nothing. That's the whole of what we're for."
Osk: "No Keeper blessed that bell, and it rings anyway. Maybe the rite was never the point. Maybe just remembering was."
You told me my verses were worth saying. I have said them since, over my own family, badly and out loud.
You called the rites superstition, once. I said them anyway, over my own family. I still don't know which of us was right.
I told you I say the verses even when I'm not sure they're heard. This is where I find out for certain.
I'm all right. The Church says the body is a borrowed coat; mine is a little torn, that's all.
The old pilgrim stair, and no fire behind us the whole climb. This is the road I would have chosen, if anyone asks a novice. — Lys: "Nobody usually does. For what it's worth, I'd have chosen it too."
I said a verse over you before you were even properly still. A waste of a good verse, since you got up anyway. — Lys: "Save it for someone who needs it more. I heard every word."

Another hollow burned instead of rested. Whatever rites might have been said there are just ash now. — Tamsin: "Ash doesn't come back for seconds. A door left open might. I know which one lets me sleep."
She has earned your trust with a hammer. I seem to have lost mine with words alone. There is a lesson in that. — Tamsin: "Do less talking about being good. Do more of the actual thing."

Rested properly, the whole rite said. That is the part that matters, whatever the ledgers end up recording. — Vell: "The rite mattered to the dead. The ledger matters to whoever asks afterward if it was true."
I trust you plainly, and you extend me none of it back. I have made my peace with that. Mostly. — Vell: "Trust is a ledger I balance slowly. Yours is noted. Not yet due."
You never once asked me to justify the Church to you. I keep waiting for the argument that never comes. — Tamsin: "I judge what you do, not what you believe. Save us both the argument."
You never ask what I believe. Only what I have read. I think that might be its own kind of respect. — Vell: "It is. Beliefs change hourly. What you've read tends to stay put."
From a chapel's own altar. I don't have a verse for that kind of taking.
You said the boy's name over the water alone. No bell, no Prior. My mother's rite was much the same, when it finally came. It counts. I promise you it counts.
The rite was for the congregation. The Priory said that for forty years about everyone the water took who wasn't on its roll. I hoped we'd stopped saying it.
Nets in the nave. My family's water. I know the dead don't need it; I said the same once, to make a burning easier. It wasn't true then either.
Some water stays a grave. Thank you for saying it to her, so I didn't have to. I'm not sure I could have kept my voice level.
You still think it was only cruelty. Maybe. It was also the only order I had left, the day the water took everyone's names.
Thank you, again, for not making me relitigate the Priory every mile since Fenmarch.
Twice now the fire's decided what should have been a rite. I can't keep calling that mercy. — Tamsin: "Nobody's asking you to call it anything. It worked. Twice." They both look at you.
Another one. I said I wouldn't stand at a third fire and call it a rite. I meant it, not just said it.
I still say a verse for every fire we didn't stop. Even the ones you'd call sense.

You had the Vale's barrow sealed. Grief needs air to go somewhere, and now there's none. — Tamsin: "Air doesn't stop a thing from climbing back out. The living get the safer door." They both look at you.
Thank you, still, for that. Some things shouldn't need defending twice.
The door's shut. I still say a verse at the stone, some days, on the way past.
Thank you. Some things a man should get to keep between himself and his god.
Every city since Emberfall, I think of that confession sitting in someone's ledger, out of his hands for good now.
Canoness Fane's own order, read back to a prior until he confessed it. My own Church, in that first fire. I have no verse ready for that yet.
A quiet truce instead of a reckoning, twice now. Maybe that is mercy. It still itches like a rite left half-said.
That carving found me a world from here, before I even knew this water existed. I still do not know what to make of that.
Four times now. I stopped finding verses for it at two. I'm running out of silences too.
Coldpass already, and I never said the rite over my own family. Fenmarch's behind us now. That door's mine, left shut.
Forty years unburied and unremarked. I don't know which was the worse sin — letting them die, or forgetting after. — Lys: "Forgetting's easier to fix. Go on, then. Nobody's stopping you."

The drowned nave rests. My family rests with it, and I'd rather the water stayed be, not charted for a ledger. — Vell: "Four centuries of parish record, Osk. That's not nothing either." They both look at you.
Thank you, still, for that. The water gets to just be quiet, for once.
Every ledger since Fenmarch, I wonder if my family reads as a footnote to someone.
Thank you, still, for that. Even a guilty man gets to grieve without an audience.
Every gallery since, I think of Aldous's face when the truth finally landed on it.
Thank you, still, for that. Some promises are worth keeping on their own terms.
The ditches matter. I only meant the promise mattered too. We agreed more than it sounded.
The Keepers' first Hall, under the water. The Priory never taught that it existed. I'm learning how much the Priory never taught.
A vow made to the dead over their own table. The Priory would call that presumption. I call it the most honest thing I've watched you do.
The covenant was the compact between the living and the dead, and we cracked it for kindling. I said a verse over the pieces. It felt like apology.
An almonry that keeps a ledger of the worthy. I have handed out bread from one of those. I never asked to see the book.
The order was the Reeve's, but the ledger was ours, and you read both aloud. I will say a verse at that barn every year I have left.
The Hunger Barn is ash, and the ledger of the worthy with it. I should feel absolved. I feel like a page was torn out.
I have stopped counting. I have not stopped noticing, and neither has anyone we pass.
A hunt's chapel with a hermit in it. The Church forgot this place, or hid it. I am learning those are the same thing.
A recall, and they came home. Not a rite, not a verse: three notes on a horn. I should be troubled that it worked. I'm only glad.
The huntsmen never got their recall, and now they never will. I said a verse over the ash. Nobody in it was listening anymore.
A chantry that buried no one because it could not bury everyone. I understand the rule. I am starting to hate the rule.
Truce. Not a rite, not a verse — a man walking out with a rod and the right words. The dead wanted so little. We gave them nothing for four hundred years.
The ground left to them, and Harrowfield shorter of bread for it. The Church would call that a fair tithe. I've stopped saying what the Church would call things.
Men who chose a sealed door over a lie. The Church calls that pride. I am not sure the Church has the right word for it.
The vault kept, and the king's face struck above it. A town that spends its dead's coin and means it as respect. I keep turning that over.
The door's through and the hoard is solder. The moneyers wanted one thing in four hundred years, and we took it to a furnace. I said the words anyway.
A fast four hundred years long, kept for a feast the Church blessed the night it was poisoned. The chantry never says which part it is fasting for.
The third toast. The Church had the rite and not the words, four hundred years. A cider-wife had the words. I'll remember that when the Church tells me what it knows.
The hall kept shut, and the first pressing carried to its doors. A fast turned into a tithe. I can't tell yet whether that's mercy or habit.
A promise carried to a door every year, and you saw that it was one. I'll remember that you did.
Fed first, and the door gets what's left, if anything is. That's how a fast ends: not broken. Forgotten.
A Church almonry once kept a ledger of who deserved to eat. I have never been proud of that page. — Tamsin: "Then be glad someone finally reads it aloud instead of just filing it."
The tithe barn, and the ledger that decided who it fed. Two duties, and I am not sure either one was mercy. — Vell: "Duties rarely are, once you read the fine print underneath them."
A hunt mustered and never recalled, four hundred years unspoken over. I don't think anyone thought it needed a rite. — Tamsin: "Nobody thought the horn needed fixing either, until you did."

Charcoal-smoke over ridings cut for a king's hunt. Whatever grief lives in this wood, nobody in four centuries thought to name it. — Vell: "Someone did, once. He just never sent for it. That someone was mine."

A shield-wall broken by dark, a charter signed before the herald's blood was cold. I want to meet whichever priest has buried nobody here. — Tamsin: "That charter's why the Companies answer to a captain, not a crown."

Two lines unburied four hundred years, and a chantry a mile off has buried neither. Grief gets swept to worse ground. — Vell: "My own line's fault, this one. I hired the men who broke that wall by blood I never chose."

Cinder-oil again, and another door that will never open to answer for what happened behind it. I don't think fire is an apology. — Tamsin: "It isn't meant as one. It's meant to end a thing an apology never would have."

A truce called at last, not one word of it mine to say. I'm glad regardless — some rites need no collar to be real. — Vell: "This one needed no priest. Just the rod, the words, and someone willing to walk them at dusk."

The almonry's ledger marked half these names unworthy before any seal touched that door. A record won't feed a soul. — Vell: "A name kept can't be starved twice. I want them written down." They both look at you.
Still glad I said it. A ledger never once fed anyone; I'll not pretend a new one would.
Written down properly. Fine. Tell me when ink has ever once opened a barn door.

leaves.say: You burned it. My family, the nave, all of it. I have nothing left to say to you.
I came to this Church to be better than my worst assumptions about people. Standing next to you keeps proving them right. I'm done.
You keep choosing the boy who isn't there over the men who still are. I need distance from that kind of certainty. I'm sorry.
Every fire since, you've stood on her side of it. I can't keep calling this company mine and mean it. I'm sorry.
You handed a dying man's confession to history before he was even cold about giving it himself. I can't square that with anything I still believe.

topics.label: who are you
topics.say: Brother Osk, of the Gray Church — a novice still, whatever the robe suggests. I'm told my verses need work. I'm told a lot of things.

topics.label: your own family
topics.say: The water took my family in Fenmarch, before I ever wore this gray. I came here to learn what to say over the drowned. Nobody's finished teaching me yet.

topics.label: why the Church, and why you
topics.say: Someone has to sit with grief and mean it. I wasn't much good at anything else, so — here I am, still learning to mean it properly.

topics.label: what you make of the gray
topics.say: Grief that's never given air festers. That's the whole of Church teaching on it, and I believe every word — I just don't always know how to open the door.

topics.label: come with me
topics.say: ...Truly? Then — yes. Purpose is easier to find walking than kneeling, some days.

topics.label: wait here (leaves the party for now)
topics.say: I'll keep this ground quiet while you're gone. It's what I'm for, mostly.

topics.label: ask him to come back
topics.say: No. You burned the nave with my family still unrested inside it. I have no verse left that forgives that, and I've stopped looking for one.

topics.label: ask him to come back
topics.say: ...The Church teaches forgiveness. I'm meant to practice what I preach, badly as I preach it. I'll come.

topics.label: ask him to come back
topics.say: Not yet. I need to believe it before I follow it. Show me: stand with the priory's counsel, or say a rite over someone who needs one. Then ask again.

topics.label: ask what he really believes
topics.say: Some nights I'm not sure the old king even hears the verses. I say them anyway. Faith, near as I can tell, is doing it anyway.

topics.label: ask why he won't meet your eye
topics.say: Because I keep hoping you'll surprise me, and you keep not doing it. That's a hard thing to say to someone's face. There. Said it.

topics.label: tell him his verses are worth saying
topics.say: Word reaches the chapel: his family's found, in the drowned nave, past hoping for but not past grieving. You tell him his verses are worth saying, badly or not. He almost smiles.

topics.label: tell him the rites are superstition
topics.say: Word reaches the chapel: his family's found, in the drowned nave, past hoping for but not past grieving. You tell him the old rites are just superstition. He goes very quiet, and doesn't answer.

topics.label: ask after his family
topics.say: They're at rest. He said the rite himself, voice cracking on the third verse, and didn't stop. I think he's a priest now, whatever the Church calls it officially.

topics.label: ask after his family
topics.say: The nave burned with them still in it. He hasn't quoted a verse since. I'm not sure he believes in doors anymore, open or shut.

topics.label: ask what he really remembers of that day
topics.say: I wasn't there when the water took them. Sent off for dry wood on some errand nobody even remembers giving me now. I have never told a living soul I sometimes wonder if that's the only reason I'm still here.

topics.label: ask if he blames himself
topics.say: Every night, some, if I'm honest — and I'm trying, for once, to be. The verses I'm learning are as much for me as for anyone drowned. Thank you for asking it plain.

topics.label: let him teach you the steadying litany
topics.say: Here, then — the litany the old priest said before hard work, not holy exactly, just steady. Say it under your breath and your hand won't shake when it matters most.
fx: "You told me my verses were worth saying, badly or not. I say this one for you, then."
"You called the rites superstition, once. I still believe them. I just stopped explaining why to you."

topics.label: back him against the priory's counsel
topics.say: I didn't ask you to cross the Priory for me. You did it anyway, plain and public, and they'll remember whose voice said it. That costs you something I can't give back to you.

topics.label: side with him — it's not his roll-book
topics.say: Thank you. I can't undo four hundred years of that roll alone. — Lys, not looking at either of you: "No. Just the one boy. That would have done."

topics.label: tell him it's not yours to judge (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly the sexton's roll isn't a fight for you to referee.
fx: "...Fair. It was between me and the Priory before she ever heard the boy's name." — Lys just shrugs, already watching the road again.
Neither wanted that answer. — Lys mutters something about people who won't pick a side; you get only silence back from him, which is worse.

topics.label: leave it between them
topics.say: You tell Lys and Brother Osk it's theirs to settle, and step back. They settle it the way people do: quietly, badly, and without you. Neither asks you again.

topics.label: back Osk — the rite still matters
topics.say: Thank you. It matters more, hearing someone else say so. — Tamsin just shrugs and goes back to her whetstone.

topics.label: back Osk — a confession isn't a chapter
topics.say: Thank you. He gave that to his god, not to history. — Vell says nothing, already composing the sentence anyway.

topics.label: tell him it's not yours to grade (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly the prior's confession isn't a fight for you to settle between them.
fx: "...That's fair. It should have been his choice from the start." — Vell, after a moment: "Fair. Noted. Not forgotten."
You go quiet in the way that means you mind. — Vell writes something down without saying what.

topics.label: leave it between them
topics.say: You tell Brother Osk and Vell it's theirs to settle, and step back. They settle it the way people do: quietly, badly, and without you. Neither asks you again.

topics.label: back Osk — the barrow needs the air
topics.say: Thank you. Some things shouldn't have to argue for room to breathe. — Tamsin just shakes her head, unconvinced.

topics.label: call the door's fate a draw (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly the barrow door isn't yours to fight over between them.
fx: "...Fair. The door's shut either way now." — Tamsin, almost gracious: "Wasn't going to keep arguing stone."
Neither wanted to let it go that easily. — Osk and Tamsin go quiet, in the way that means they mean to keep disagreeing, just not out loud.

topics.label: leave it between them
topics.say: You tell Brother Osk and Tamsin it's theirs to settle, and step back. They settle it the way people do: quietly, badly, and without you. Neither asks you again.

topics.label: that's enough — go in peace
topics.say: Go in peace, truly. I don't say that lightly, and I have not said it to just anyone.

topics.label: that's enough — go carefully
topics.say: Go carefully. I'll say a verse regardless of how this ends between the two of us.

topics.label: that's enough — this city is heavy
topics.say: Go gently. Four hundred years of grief under these streets, and I'm trying not to feel all of it at once.

topics.label: that's enough for now
topics.say: Go gently. The gray doesn't need help from us to be cruel.

topics.label: back Osk — leave the water be
topics.say: Thank you. Some graves don't need a second visit. — Vell says nothing, already composing the sentence anyway.

topics.label: back Osk — shame isn't the same as rest
topics.say: Thank you. Even a guilty man's grief needs somewhere to go that isn't a crowd. — Tamsin just shrugs and goes back to her whetstone.

topics.label: tell them it's not yours to weigh (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly what Aldous deserves isn't a verdict for you to hand down between them.
fx: "Fine. He answered for it. That's the arithmetic closed." — Osk, quiet: "I hope closed isn't the same as finished, for him."
Neither of you looks satisfied. — Osk says a verse under his breath; Tamsin just checks the edge on her hammer.

topics.label: leave it between them
topics.say: You tell Brother Osk and Tamsin it's theirs to settle, and step back. They settle it the way people do: quietly, badly, and without you. Neither asks you again.

topics.label: back Osk — the promise still counts
topics.say: Thank you. A kept promise doesn't need to fix everything to be worth keeping. — Lys just shrugs, still watching the water.

topics.label: tell them it's not yours to weigh (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly what the covenant is worth now isn't a fight for you to settle between them.
fx: "...Fair. It was Maren's promise before it was ours to weigh." — Osk, quiet: "Fair. I can carry that much unresolved."
Neither wanted that answer. — Lys watches the water; Osk says a verse under his breath, for no one in particular.

topics.label: leave it between them
topics.say: You tell Lys and Brother Osk it's theirs to settle, and step back. They settle it the way people do: quietly, badly, and without you. Neither asks you again.

topics.label: back Osk — a fast kept on purpose
topics.say: Good. A fast Mootcombe chose is worth more than one it was handed. — Lys says nothing, just counts the rows she can see from here.

topics.label: call the pressing a draw (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly whether Mootcombe feeds its dead or its living isn't yours to settle between them.
fx: "...Fair. It's Mootcombe's fast, not mine." — Osk, quieter: "Nor mine to keep for them."
Neither wanted that answer. — Lys goes to look at the rows; Osk says the office under his breath, done with the talk.

topics.label: leave it between them
topics.say: You tell Lys and Osk it's theirs to settle, and step back. They settle it the way people do: quietly, badly, and without you. Neither asks you again.

topics.label: call it a draw between them (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly this fire isn't yours to referee.
fx: "Fine. Wasn't going to stop swinging a hammer over a novice's feelings anyway." — Osk, dry for once: "Noted, with love."
You're as bad as the rest of the ditherers, near as Tamsin's concerned. — Osk just looks at the ground and doesn't argue the word.

topics.label: call it a draw between them (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly the drowned nave isn't a fight for you to settle between them.
fx: "...Fair. It was Fenmarch's grief before it was your footnote." — Vell, almost gracious: "Noted. I can wait."
Neither of you looks satisfied. — Vell taps the notebook shut, and doesn't open it again today.

topics.label: back Osk — no ledger feeds the living
topics.say: Good. Somebody should say plainly that paper never once fed a crofter. — Vell only makes a note, unconvinced but careful about it.

topics.label: call the record a draw (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly whether the barn's dead get a record or a rite isn't yours to settle between them.
fx: "...Fair. The ledger was ours to answer for, not yours." — Vell, after a moment: "Fair. Noted. Not forgotten."
Neither wanted that answer. — Osk says a verse under his breath; Vell writes something down without saying what.

tamsin.name: Tamsin
tamsin.desc: Forge-scarred hands at the second anvil, keeping time with the smith's without missing a stroke.
onDeath: Tamsin goes down at the second anvil, mid-swing. The smith will have to find new hands for that hammer.

remarks.say: Cinderhall's burning. Whatever's left of the truth about that mine burns with it. Convenient, that.
Good. Grief that won't quit gets put down, same as anything else that won't quit.
You walked away and settled nothing. That's the one option I'd have talked you out of, if you'd asked.
He's quiet now. Didn't need killing after all. Fine — I'll take an ending that doesn't cost a fight, when one's on offer.
Broke the crown. Good — less for the next fool to fight over.
Sealed for good. That's a door that'll hold. I checked the hinges myself.
Free Company work, this ground. Mercenaries. I've sharpened enough of their blades to know their word's worth exactly what they're paid.
Wet ground ruins good steel fast. Whatever you're carrying, dry it tonight.
Watch country. Say what you like about rules — their gear's always in good repair. I respect that.
Cinderhall. Home ground, near enough. I know this air. Iron and old smoke.
Barrows everywhere you look. Keepers guard the dead like the dead are still paying them. Maybe they are.
Salt eats steel worse than anything. Remind me to check every blade we're carrying before we leave.
Cold enough up here to crack a bad weld. Whoever forged your gear better have known what they were doing.
Ground gone to glass. Whatever burned this hot, it burned hotter than any forge I've ever worked.
Four fires before yours, and it only ever sang louder after. I still believe in fire. I'm starting to believe this one valley just doesn't.
Marrowgate. Big walls, soft hands, near as I can tell. We'll see if that holds up.
Three hollows settled without burning a one of them. Didn't think that was the harder road. Turns out it was.
You've earned my back. That's not a small thing, coming from me.
One more like that and I'm gone. I don't give second warnings, only first ones.
I don't waste time on people I don't trust. I'm starting to wonder why I'm still wasting it on you.
Cinderhall's settled without burning. Did not think that was possible down there. Good to be wrong.
Bargained instead of burned. Not clean, but it holds. I can live with not-clean, if it holds.
Whoever lied about that collapse answered for it. I did not need to swing a hammer. Strange feeling.
I let it lie. Chasing it was not bringing her back. Took me long enough to admit that plainly.
They sold out the men still working that mine. For coin. I do not have words for that. I have a hammer.
Inside the palace. Big walls, soft floors. I keep waiting for someone to ask us to leave.
You took her oil and her bargain both. Fine. Just do not forget whose name goes on it after.
You said no to a Regent's offer. Did not flinch either, near as I could tell. Good.
He said it plain, finally. Four hundred years is a long time to swing at nothing.
Tamsin: "Debt was paid all along, and the company just never said. That's the kind of lie that costs nothing to fix and everything to leave."
You told me to make them answer for it. I did. Or I let it lie. Either way, you said it, and I heard it.
You called it wasted iron, once. Maybe it was. I chased it anyway, or I didn't. Either way, you said it, and I heard it.
I told you I've been counting blows since I was twelve. This is where the counting stops, one way or another.
Twelve years counting blows and I still let that one through. It won't happen twice.
Home ground. Smells like the forge and worse things. The good paths here are worn by miners who did not watch their footing. — Lys: "I'll watch the ground. You watch whatever's watching you back."
I would trust you at my back tomorrow. She is still deciding. Give her time, or don't; either way I am not budging. — Lys: "Still deciding is not the same as deciding against."
A Regent's writ got us through that gate. Paid for in fire, but paid, and we are through it. — Osk: "I keep counting what that writ actually cost. The sum troubles me more the longer I add it up."
You went down easier than I'd like from someone who spends half his day sweeping. Eat something. — Osk: "The Church does not train for combat. It trains for enduring what combat leaves behind."

You still have not decided about her. I decided in a day. Slow is not always wiser, near as I have seen. — Vell: "Slow has kept me alive this long. I'd rather be right eventually than quick and wrong."
It is a chair. Old, ugly, and everyone's died over it regardless. I do not understand the fuss, honestly. — Vell: "The fuss is four hundred years and my own name buried somewhere in it."
You move quiet for someone carrying that much steel. I only just noticed. — Lys: "You move loud for someone who notices everything else. Fair trade, I'd say."
You talk like every word costs you coin. I talk like I am paying for someone else's silence. We will manage. — Vell: "An astute observation, for someone who claims not to care for words."
You don't lift a keeper's own goods from under their nose. That's not clever. That's just taking.
That's my old master's iron gone missing. Put it back, or don't call yourself square with that forge again.
The vigil's off. The Hundred got a promise out of Cinderhall and it lasted a season. I have kept longer watches for men I liked less.
A warden's wage, so no lad loses his sleep to the dead. That is how a watch is meant to be kept: paid, and by someone who chose it.
The scratches stay, and the company's sign stays over them. You could have given the Hundred a stone. Never mind. Someone with a chisel will, one night.
A cairn on ground the Watch earned honestly. Four hundred years guarding a thief's road, and the first true stone goes up in my lifetime. I'll take that.
The garrison eats thin so the patrols keep walking. Nobody made them. That's the Watch I joined, when I was fool enough to think it was the only kind.
You paid the Watch's shortfall out of your own purse. The quartermaster will never trust it. I do. Don't make a habit of carrying us, though.
Rites are for people with time to spare. I still don't have any.
Didn't need the vote of confidence. I'll take it anyway.
Soft is how camps rot. I'll say it as many times as it takes to be wrong about it.
Camp's harder now, and your brother's still in it. If that rope's ever pointed his way, you'll find me standing in front of it.
Watch still stands the wall the same, lie or no lie. Good. That's what matters to the men on it.
Hope your true history's worth what it costs the next recruit who believed in that wall.

The Vale's barrow left open to the sky, after everything that hill let out. That's not mercy, just careless. — Osk: "Grief manages worse behind a shut door too. I'd rather careless than cruel." They both look at you.
Good. One less door for something to wander back out of.
Open to the sky. Fine. I'll be the one checking that hill every season, then.
Aldous's own truth, pulled plain instead of beaten out of him. That's the kind of dealing I trust, soldier or scholar.
You stood your own watch, then settled it yourself, no Keeper's blessing needed. That's authority the plain way — earned, not worn.
A captain and a sergeant, different colors, same read on you at a glance. Soldiers know soldiers. I'd take that over a medal.
Three. I said I don't give second warnings. Consider this the sound of me counting, not warning.
Four times, from under people's noses. You've had all the words you're getting out of me on it.
I've stopped counting. That should worry you more than the counting did.
Cinderhall's behind us, and I still don't know who lied about that collapse. That's mine to finish. Not yours to carry.
Cinderhall's behind us. I know who lied about that collapse now, and I haven't decided what that's worth. That's mine to finish. Not yours to carry.
Forty years empty, and the Crown still calls it property instead of a grave. — Vell: "Escheat is exactly that, dressed in law. I've made a study of that particular dressing."
Camp still holds. Didn't need the vote of confidence, but I'll take it.
Soft is how a toll-road gets robbed blind. I'll say it as many times as it takes.

The Hundred rest now, the truth about Aldous said plain over their own grave. He earned every word of that shame. — Osk: "Shame doesn't rest anyone, Tamsin. It only moves the grief around." They both look at you.
Didn't need the vote of confidence on Aldous. I'll take it anyway.
Rest doesn't un-ring what he did. I'll say that as many times as it takes.
Didn't need the vote of confidence on the chandler. I'll take it anyway.
Scholars worry about rings. I worry about the living who'd sell their own teeth for less.
Wet ground, wet timber, wet everything. Nothing here I'd know how to fix, and everyone still standing anyway. Fair enough.
Charges under four hundred years of water, and the stone came up in three. Fire did what it does. I'll not pretend it did it clean.
A stone's a stone. But you spoke three words over it and the water sat down. I'll take that over charges, this once.
A tithe barn with a Watch sergeant on the steps. Somebody worked out long ago that grain needs guarding more than gold does.
The barn's open. That's arithmetic somebody will have to do every winter now, not just once. I hope Tithing can count.
Old timber goes up fast. The bailiff will call it an accident by the time the ash is cold, and the Regent will call it farmland.
Charcoal. Every forge in Cinderhall eats this wood by the cartload, and I never once asked where the carts came from.
The rides stay open one night a year and the burners lose a night's sleep. Cheap, for what the forges get. I'd have taken that deal myself.
The Stand's gone and the coppice will follow. The forges will thank you. I find I've stopped counting that as the only kind of thanks.
So this is where the Companies were born. Every sergeant at Highward has a speech about it: hired swords and a herald shot. The Watch takes no one's coin. That's the whole speech.
A field given up to the dead. Good iron under it too, the picker says. Somebody always pays for a truce; this time it's a village's bread.
Cinder-oil on a battlefield. The bosses will come out of the ash by the cartload, and the Ironbound will thank you. I keep finding I don't want their thanks.
A water-race for the hammers. Whoever built that mint knew their trade; the Watch pays its smiths in Pennywell silver, and I never once looked at the face.
Both dies and a clean strike. I'd have given a year's wages to hold that hammer. You did it without shaking; I noticed.
Sealed, and struck above it with the old face. Good silver stays good whatever's on it. The Crown will hate it, which is a point in its favour.
A safe-conduct given at a table and broken at the door. The Watch was founded against exactly that, or so Highward says. Highward says a lot.
They got their toast and they rose. A word kept four hundred years late is still a word kept. I'd drink to that, if I drank the cider here.
You burned the hall with the cooper's oil. His casks, his fire, his hall's timber gone with it. The Ironbound will call that thrift. I'm trying not to.

Four sacks in ten to the Crown, same as it's run four hundred years. Somebody does that math and never asks who goes hungry for it. — Vell: "I've read the Crown's own math on this tithe. It never once shows its work."

Every forge in Cinderhall eats this wood by the cartload, and I never once asked whose hunt it used to be. — Vell: "Mine, near enough. My own first ancestor's father's hunt, riding on your charcoal money now."

The Companies were born on this ground, out of a broken truce and someone's itchy trigger-finger. — Vell: "My own ancestor's trigger-finger, near enough. I have never said that plainly to anyone before you."
The Companies' charter was signed the night a herald was shot asking truce. The Watch takes no coin for its wall. — Vell: "My line hired them. No lord would ride that winter." They both look at you.
Still glad I said it. The Watch never once took a coin for that wall, then or now.
Honest coin. Right. Ask the herald's line what an honest sword bought them.
Cinderhall's hearths stay lit either way. Didn't need the vote of confidence, but I'll take it.
Soft is how a forge goes cold. I'll say it as many times as it takes.

leaves.say: You sold out the miners. The same mine that killed my mother, and you sold out the men still working it for coin. We're done.
I don't fight beside people I can't trust at my back. That's you now. Find someone else.
You'd rather a verse than a done thing, every time it costs something. I don't have patience left for that arithmetic.
You'll keep that glade soft until it costs someone living. I've buried enough people who trusted soft. Find another hammer.
You handed the Watch's own lie to whoever asks now, recruits included. I've seen what losing faith in the wall does to a garrison. I want no part of causing it.

topics.label: who are you
topics.say: Smith's apprentice. Ask me about steel and I'll talk your ear off. Ask me about anything else, keep it short.

topics.label: what you actually want
topics.say: Ask the smith and she'll tell you not to say 'mine' near me. I'm saying it anyway: the Hundred came down on my mother in the Iron Downs, and nobody's ever given me a straight answer why.

topics.label: what you make of the gray
topics.say: Grief's not complicated. Something's wrong, you find what's wrong, you fix it or you burn it. People make it complicated because plain answers scare them.

topics.label: come with me
topics.say: Good. I've been itching to hit something that isn't an anvil.

topics.label: wait here (leaves the party for now)
topics.say: Fine. Don't get yourself killed doing something I could've done faster.

topics.label: ask her to come back
topics.say: No. You sold out men working the same mine that killed my mother, for coin, and you want me to forget that. I don't forget. Ever.

topics.label: ask her to come back
topics.say: ...You've done enough to earn a second look. Don't waste it.

topics.label: ask her to come back
topics.say: Not yet. Show me, don't tell me.

topics.label: ask what really drives her
topics.say: I was twelve when the Hundred came down and they carried what was left of my mother out of that shaft. I've been counting blows ever since — needed something I could measure.

topics.label: ask what she thinks of you
topics.say: You want it straight? I think you talk more than you act, and I've got no use for people like that. There. Straight.

topics.label: tell her to make them answer for it
topics.say: The truth about the mine comes out at last, uglier than she guessed. You tell her to make whoever's responsible answer for it. She nods once, already working out how.

topics.label: tell her chasing it wastes good iron
topics.say: The truth about the mine comes out at last, uglier than she guessed. You tell her chasing it further wastes good iron and better time. Something in her jaw sets hard.

topics.label: ask about the mine
topics.say: Whoever lied about that collapse has answered for it now, her way — plain, and final. She doesn't talk about it much. Doesn't need to.

topics.label: ask about the mine
topics.say: She let it lie, in the end. Said carrying it further wouldn't carry her mother back. First time I've heard her sound tired instead of angry.

topics.label: ask about the miners
topics.say: The miners got sold out to the Ironbound for a tidy sum, truth and all, buried under it. She hasn't said a word since she heard. That's worse than shouting.

topics.label: ask what she still expects, some days
topics.say: Some mornings I still listen for her boots on the forge steps. Twenty years gone and some fool part of me hasn't caught up with the rest. Never told the smith that. Never told anyone.

topics.label: ask why she never told the smith
topics.say: She'd worry, and worrying doesn't temper steel. Counting does. So I count, and I don't tell her, and most days that's enough to get the hammer swinging again.

topics.label: let her re-temper your blade
topics.say: Hand it over. Won't take long done right. There — feel that edge now. It won't turn on you when it matters most, and neither will I.
fx: "You told me to make them answer for it. I did. This edge remembers that too."
"You called it wasted iron, once. Maybe. I tempered this blade anyway."

topics.label: cross the Ironbound to back her question
topics.say: You put the question to the Ironbound chapter yourself, plain and public, and didn't back down when they didn't like it. They'll mark your name for it. I'm not going to say thank you. I don't have to.

topics.label: back Tamsin — burn it and be done
topics.say: Good. Someone with sense. — Osk doesn't argue, just goes quiet in the way that means he's still arguing, inside.

topics.label: tell her to leave this one to him (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly this fire isn't yours to referee.
fx: "Fine. Wasn't going to stop swinging a hammer over a novice's feelings anyway." — Osk, dry for once: "Noted, with love."
You're as bad as the rest of the ditherers, near as Tamsin's concerned. — Osk just looks at the ground and doesn't argue the word.

topics.label: leave it between them
topics.say: You tell Brother Osk and Tamsin it's theirs to settle, and step back. They settle it the way people do: quietly, badly, and without you. Neither asks you again.

topics.label: back her — the camp needs its teeth
topics.say: Good. Soft camps bury more men than hard ones do. — Lys says nothing, just watches the west road longer than usual.

topics.label: back Tamsin — the Watch keeps its honor
topics.say: Good. Those men on the wall never lied to anyone. Let them keep believing in something. — Vell looks like they've lost an argument they didn't know was still running.

topics.label: tell her it's not yours to settle (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly the fort's founding isn't a fight for you to settle between them.
fx: "...Fine. Wasn't my lie to begin with." — Vell, almost gracious: "Nor mine to force on people still standing that wall."
You're as bad as a politician, near as Tamsin's concerned. — Vell says nothing, which from Vell is its own verdict.

topics.label: leave it between them
topics.say: You tell Tamsin and Vell it's theirs to settle, and step back. They settle it the way people do: quietly, badly, and without you. Neither asks you again.

topics.label: back Tamsin — the barrow should hold
topics.say: Good. Someone ought to think about who's still walking past that hill. — Osk says nothing, just looks back the way of the Vale a while.

topics.label: that's enough — square between us
topics.say: Watch your footing anyway. Habit now, not doubt — you've earned better than doubt from me.

topics.label: that's enough for now, plainly
topics.say: Watch your footing. That part doesn't change regardless of what I currently think of you.

topics.label: that's enough — soft floors here
topics.say: Watch your footing. Different ground in this city — the kind that gives out quiet, not loud.

topics.label: that's enough for now
topics.say: Watch your footing. I'm not carrying you back.

topics.label: back Tamsin — the discipline held
topics.say: Good. A Company that faces its own dead honest won't lie to you about coin either. — Lys says nothing, just watches the west road longer than usual.

topics.label: call the toll-road a draw (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly what Camp Gallows charges on the road isn't yours to referee between them.
fx: "...Fair. Wasn't my ledger to begin with." — Tamsin, almost gracious: "Nor mine to make you keep."
Neither wanted that answer. — Lys watches the road; Tamsin goes back to her whetstone, done with the talk.

topics.label: leave it between them
topics.say: You tell Lys and Tamsin it's theirs to settle, and step back. They settle it the way people do: quietly, badly, and without you. Neither asks you again.

topics.label: back Tamsin — Aldous had it coming
topics.say: Good. Someone should say his name the way the mine says my mother's. — Osk says nothing, just watches the gallery mouth a while longer.

topics.label: back Tamsin — coin outlasts grief
topics.say: Good. The dead kings never once fed a chandler's family. — Vell makes a note, unconvinced but careful about it.

topics.label: tell them it's not yours to price (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly what leaves the barrows isn't a fight for you to settle between them.
fx: "...Fine. Wasn't my counter to police anyway." — Vell, almost gracious: "Nor mine to shut on people who need the coin."
Neither wanted that answer. — Tamsin goes back to her gear; Vell writes something down without saying what.

topics.label: leave it between them
topics.say: You tell Tamsin and Vell it's theirs to settle, and step back. They settle it the way people do: quietly, badly, and without you. Neither asks you again.

topics.label: call it a draw between them (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly the glade's rope isn't a fight for you to settle between them.
fx: "...Fair. It was Vane's camp before it was my brother's problem." — Tamsin grunts something that might be agreement.
You'd let the wolves vote on the sheep pen too, near as Lys is concerned. — Tamsin just goes back to her whetstone, done with the talk.

topics.label: call it a draw between them (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly the barrow door isn't yours to fight over between them.
fx: "...Fair. The door's shut either way now." — Tamsin, almost gracious: "Wasn't going to keep arguing stone."
Neither wanted to let it go that easily. — Osk and Tamsin go quiet, in the way that means they mean to keep disagreeing, just not out loud.

topics.label: call it a draw between them (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly what Aldous deserves isn't a verdict for you to hand down between them.
fx: "Fine. He answered for it. That's the arithmetic closed." — Osk, quiet: "I hope closed isn't the same as finished, for him."
Neither of you looks satisfied. — Osk says a verse under his breath; Tamsin just checks the edge on her hammer.

topics.label: back Tamsin — the forges have to eat
topics.say: Good. A coppice cut fair keeps Cinderhall's hearths lit without anyone starving for it. — Lys says nothing, just watches the treeline longer than usual.

topics.label: call the coppice a draw (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly whether the Kingswood feeds a hearth or a hunt isn't yours to settle between them.
fx: "...Fair. It was Cinderhall's argument before it was mine to make." — Tamsin, almost gracious: "Nor mine to make you keep."
Neither wanted that answer. — Lys watches the treeline; Tamsin goes back to counting cords, done with the talk.

topics.label: leave it between them
topics.say: You tell Lys and Tamsin it's theirs to settle, and step back. They settle it the way people do: quietly, badly, and without you. Neither asks you again.

topics.label: back Tamsin — an honest wall owes no one
topics.say: Good. Someone should say the Watch's way costs less than it looks. — Vell makes a note, unconvinced but careful about it.

topics.label: call the charter a draw (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly whose coin bought the Shieldings' peace isn't yours to settle between them.
fx: "...Fair. It was the Watch's pride talking, not the field's." — Vell, after a moment: "Fair. Noted. Not forgotten."
Neither wanted that answer. — Tamsin goes back to counting the field's iron; Vell writes something down without saying what.

vell.name: Vell
vell.desc: A traveller in road-worn gray, a book open by the fire, unbothered by much.
onDeath: Vell falls with the book still open on their knee, a sentence half-copied that no one will ever finish reading.

remarks.say: Hollowbrook's burning, and with it every record the Keepers never finished copying. That is not a small loss.
A death, unrecorded by any rite. History will remember only that he stopped being a problem. Poor epitaph.
An unfinished story. I dislike those more than sad endings. At least a sad ending is an ending.
Properly rested, properly recorded. That's the kind of ending that actually holds.
You broke it. Four hundred years of history, and you broke it. I have opinions about this I am choosing not to share yet.
Sealed away from study forever, most likely. A scholar's small grief, next to everything else that happened there.
Mercenary country. Poor record-keeping, excellent gossip. I'll take what I can get.
Fenmarch keeps its history underwater, apparently. I do hope it kept it readable.
Wardmoor's archive is meant to be excellent. I intend to find out, given half a chance.
The Ironbound burn what they don't like. I try not to think too hard about what that's cost the Downs' history.
Barrowmere. The Keepers' Hall is here somewhere. I have — reasons to want to see it.
Gullhaven keeps its records in the harbormaster's memory, near as I can tell. Frustrating, and probably more accurate than paper.
St. Ashwyn's Perch. Old enough to remember things properly, if anyone up here still bothers to ask it.
Emberfall. I'd heard the name only as a footnote before. It deserves a chapter, not a footnote.
A fifth fire, and still no one writes down that the first four already failed. I intend to be the one who finally does.
Marrowgate.
Three rites completed properly, three records worth keeping. I'm almost tempted to write this down as it happens, for once.
I don't extend trust for free. Consider this the exception, not the rule.
One more incident like that and I revise my opinion of you permanently. Consider this your only warning.
I am reconsidering several earlier assessments of your character. None of the revisions favor you.
Hollowbrook's barrow-court rests, properly recorded, I hope. I intend to check the record myself.
Bargained — the mounds settle for less than rest. An imprecise ending. I dislike those. It will have to do.
So it is found. My name is not in it — my grandfather's is. Close enough, I suppose.
I would have told you myself, eventually. Being dragged into the light is not the same as choosing it.
Inside the palace that exiled my line. I find I have opinions I am choosing not to voice yet.
You took the Regent's oil. I wonder if you understand yet whose furniture you are burning.
You refused her. I confess I did not expect that, and I dislike being wrong this pleasantly.
Four hundred years unrecorded, and now it is said aloud. I intend to write this one down properly.
Vell: "A verse carried whole between two Halls that had nearly forgotten each other existed. I intend to write this one down properly."
You told me the truth was worth knowing, whatever it cost. It cost something. I'd still rather have known.
You told me to burn it and be done. I didn't. I'm not sure yet whether that was courage or just curiosity.
I told you I'd rather you heard it from me than the throne. Here's the throne. Ask it whatever you like — I already answered.
You kept your word about my name, all the way to this room. I didn't expect that, least of all from you.
Whatever this seat decides, my own question is still unanswered. I find that easier to bear standing up.
You told her. I asked to choose the when and the who, and you chose for me. I'll remember which of us that was.
Up. I'm up. Write that down somewhere it can't be edited: I did not stay down.

Barrowmere. My answer is here somewhere, in a ledger nobody has opened in decades. I intend to be thorough. — Lys: "Thorough's fine. Just don't get so lost in the reading you forget which way is out."

My own name might be older than this throne, and I still do not know what I will do standing this close to it. — Lys: "Whatever you do, do it because you chose it, not because a crown told you who you are."
Fenmarch. Somewhere under this water is the reason you wear that gray. I will not pretend that is light to walk beside. — Osk: "It is heavier to carry alone. Walk beside it as long as you like."
Four hundred years of my own family's silence, and it ends in this room. I do not know what verse covers that. — Osk: "None of mine do either. I'll say one anyway. Silence has waited long enough."
