Barrowmere's archive holds what I have spent a lifetime not asking about. I intend to finally ask. — Tamsin: "Ask, then. Standing here wondering wastes better light than we've got."
Whatever proof I had of my own name burned with that mound. I am trying very hard not to resent you for it. — Tamsin: "Trying's more than most manage. For what it's worth, I didn't light that one."
You watch everything and say almost none of it. I find that unbearably suspicious in a person. — Lys: "Good. Keep finding it suspicious. Means you're paying attention."
Whatever that was worth, it was worth more sitting where someone could still read it.
You sent the widow to Wren instead of ruling on it yourself. Correct. A Hall's custom bends only from the inside, and only once someone stands in it and asks.
Oars off the point, once, and then not again. That was the tithe's receipt being torn up. Old debts don't wear thin, they wait. I'd have paid it.
Years of tithe paid at once. Gullhaven gets to stop arguing with itself every spring. As bookkeeping goes, that's the finest thing you've done. I mean it kindly.
Peat cut from the oath-ground. Four centuries of history, sold by the sod. I'd mind more if the history had been true. As it stands, I mind a little.
The ash stays untouched. The Watch will call it reverence; I'd call it evidence. Either way, someone a century on will be glad it's still there to read.

The prior confessed his own Church ordered that fire. That belongs in a record, not only a rite. — Osk: "He confessed it to make his peace, Vell. Not to be a chapter in your book." They both look at you.
A confession nobody may read is a confession that never quite happened. I still believe that.
The record stands because you let it. History thanks you. I'll settle for saying it myself.

Four hundred years, and the Watch has guarded a lie about its own crown. That deserves knowing. — Tamsin: "It deserves men who still show up tomorrow. Mind whose faith you're spending." They both look at you.
We're standing where that lie was born, and the Watch still doesn't know the whole of it. Some silences outlive their reasons.
Thank you. I intend to write this one down properly, as promised.
Standing here, I still think you sentimentalize bargains no one could have kept. I've mostly stopped saying so.
Thank you for not romanticizing an arrangement that was never going to hold.
No rite, no crown returned, nothing recorded — you killed him and called it finished. — Lys: "Finished is finished. I'd rather that than watching him grieve forever." They both look at you.
Thank you. I intend to treat it better than a trophy, whatever anyone assumes.
You called it just taking. Maybe. I still think proof of a bloodline outweighs tidiness.
Arguing a covenant's terms until a Keeper forgets to be wary of you — I have built a career on exactly that trick. Effective, isn't it.
You walked out of her solar with oil and her thanks, and none of it touched what I am to this palace. I noticed how carefully you managed that.
A name kept at Hollowbrook, one of the old line, living and hidden. I said very little when you learned that. I am still saying very little.
A spymaster's gossip, a herald's script — you read both the same careful way, half a Reach apart. I have kept a private tally of it.
Five things taken that were watched. I catalogue habits for a living; I know what this one is called.
Hollowbrook's behind us, and that ledger's still chained wherever it is. My own name, still unread. I can live with that a little longer.
A vow to leave the dead their fields, made and then not kept. I collect broken promises for a living. This one still costs something.

Forty years of names, gone in one more fire. Whatever the surveyor calls that ash, it won't be farmland to anyone who remembers. — Osk: "I'll say the names I recall. Not much of a rite. It's what's left to give."
The Reeve's Pride rests, and the fog's thinned enough for every wrecker in Gullhaven to strip her bare now. — Lys: "She's a wreck, Vell. Iron doesn't grieve." They both look at you.
Thank you. I intend to see that hull catalogued before Gullhaven strips it for scrap.
Iron doesn't grieve. I still do, on its behalf, apparently.
Thank you for that. I've already started the notes; the ink dries slower over water, but it dries.
A rested grave nobody may study is a grave that stays half-told. I still believe that.

The barrows rest, and Barrowmere's chandler still sells dead queens' rings off her counter same as always. — Tamsin: "Rings don't feed anyone underground. Above ground, they do." They both look at you.
Thank you, still. Someone ought to ask where a barrow-queen's ring ends up.
Coin over grief. I catalogue that particular trade for a living. I still mind it.
The Meres. The Ashreeve records mention it once, as a drainage problem. I begin to see what they were draining.
The covenant, whole, in my hands. My own line's oldest crime is written on it. I have never wanted a document more, or deserved one less.
A covenant sworn and left unread. I have spent my life on promises like that. I had hoped not to help make one.
The Hearthlands. The Vale ate that winter; the records say so. They do not say where the grain was, or who stood at the doors.
The order was in my ancestor's hand. Now it has been read where it was obeyed, and the names beside it. Write that down; I have.
My line sealed that barn, and I have helped burn it. Two Ashreeves, four hundred years apart, and neither of us opened the doors.
The Kingswood. The king's own hunt was out here the morning my ancestor took the crown. The records say the hunt was 'not recalled.' Now I know what that means.
Recalled at last, four hundred years late, by a stranger with a borrowed horn. The Ashreeves never sent for them. I have written that down.
A night a year for the hunt. My line owed them a recall and paid nothing; the burners owe them nothing and pay a night's fear. That is the Reach, in one bargain.
The Shieldings. The records call it the first Reeve's victory and give it a page. The herald has one line, unnamed: 'shot in error at dusk.' I am learning what my house's errors look like.
A truce called by a stranger with a mended rod, four hundred years after my ancestor's captain refused it. I have written the herald's name down at last.
My line broke that wall with hired swords, and now the field is ash. The Ashreeves' victory is complete. I did not think I could be more ashamed of it.
Pennywell. Every coin in the Reach carries my ancestor's face because of what happened under this town. I have spent a great many of them without thinking.
The king's penny, struck once more, four hundred years after my house mortared the door on the men who kept it. I have one in my hand. I am not sure I can spend it.
Burned through. My line took the crown, the coin, and now the vault, and I stood there while it happened. The face on the silver is still ours. I wish it were not.
Mootcombe. The Feast of Wax is the page my house tore out of every record it kept. The safe-conduct was my ancestor's word. I know what the word was worth now.
The third toast, drunk at last at the head of my ancestor's table. I stood where he stood and said the words he never meant. It is the first thing I have done in his chair.
The hall stays shut and the pressing goes to the door every year. Mootcombe feeds the guests my line poisoned. I would rather that than a stone with my name on it.
Still glad you saw it my way. A name kept is harder to starve twice.
No record, then. I keep finding this Reach prefers its dead convenient to its dead remembered.
Still glad you saw it plain. A sword that shows up beats a lord who doesn't.
No lord came that winter. I keep finding this Reach prefers its rescues tidy to its rescues real.

leaves.say: You broke the one thing that might have named me honestly, and I no longer trust you to carry what's left of the truth. I'll carry it myself.
You swore to keep my name out of it. You named it anyway, the first time it paid. I don't forget a broken oath. I'm gone.
I've reconsidered the wisdom of this arrangement entirely. Goodbye.
You buried a truth to spare a Church its discomfort. I've spent my whole life on the wrong end of exactly that habit. I'm done watching it happen.
You chose the Watch's comfort over four hundred years of an honest record. I have spent my whole life paying for exactly that choice, made by someone else. I won't watch you make it again.
You keep grading bargains by whether the dead can enforce them. Mine never could either, and I'm tired of that being the measure. I'm gone.

topics.label: who are you
topics.say: A wandering scholar, of sorts. I read old stones for a living, when the living pays. Ask me anything — I may even answer truthfully.

topics.label: what you're really after
topics.say: A particular kind of truth, buried in a particular kind of ledger. I'll say no more than that until I trust you a little further.

topics.label: why you go quiet at 'Marrowgate'
topics.say: Do I? I hadn't noticed. Some cities aren't kind to certain names. Leave it there, for now.

topics.label: what you make of the gray
topics.say: Four hundred years of neglected rites, come due all at once. Not a curse. An unpaid debt — and debts don't forget the way people do.

topics.label: come with me
topics.say: ...An excellent notion, actually. I do my best thinking while walking, and my worst while paying for a room.

topics.label: wait here (leaves the party for now)
topics.say: I'll mind the ledgers. Someone ought to, and it clearly isn't going to be you.

topics.label: ask them to come back
topics.say: ...Curiosity outweighs pride, in the end. It usually does, with me. I'll come.

topics.label: ask them to come back
topics.say: Not yet. I'd rather finish being right about you before I forgive you for it.

topics.label: ask what they're hiding
topics.say: The truth, since you've earned it: I'm Marrowgate's own blood, exiled before I could walk. The ledger in Hollowbrook proves it. I'd rather you heard it from me than the throne.

topics.label: ask what they think of you
topics.say: I think you handle the truth the way a child handles a knife — carelessly, and someone always ends up cut.

topics.label: tell them the truth is worth knowing
topics.say: The ledger surfaces at last, every line damning or vindicating, depending on the reader. You tell them the truth deserves to be known, whatever it costs. They go still, then nod.

topics.label: tell them to burn the ledger
topics.say: The ledger surfaces at last, every line damning or vindicating, depending on the reader. You tell them to burn it and be done with the whole business. Something in their face closes over.

topics.label: ask about the ledger
topics.say: The secret got out before Vell ever chose to tell it — dragged into the light at the worst possible moment. They haven't forgiven whoever did that. Might not forgive themselves either.

topics.label: ask if they've ever been to Marrowgate
topics.say: Once. Years before I met you, plain gray, nobody looking twice. I stood in the market square, looked up at the palace, and did not go in. I have never told anyone that either.

topics.label: ask why they turned back that day
topics.say: I wasn't ready to know what I'd do, standing in that hall with that name behind me. I'm still not entirely sure. I'd rather you knew that about me before either of us finds out.

topics.label: let them annotate your memory
topics.say: Hold still — this won't hurt, and it won't show. Just recall the shape of what you want to keep, and I'll mark the parts worth keeping. The right fact will surface when you need it.
fx: "You told them the truth was worth knowing. I've marked that fact particularly well."
"You told them to burn the ledger, once. I did not forget. I annotate that too, for balance."

topics.label: swear to keep their name out of it
topics.say: You gave your word, plainly, that whatever that ledger says stays between the two of us unless I choose otherwise. I don't extend trust for free, remember. Consider this noted. And remembered.

topics.label: back Vell — it belongs in the record
topics.say: Thank you. Truth shouldn't need my begging to survive. — Osk looks like something in him has quietly closed.

topics.label: back Vell — the truth outranks comfort
topics.say: Thank you. The Watch will survive knowing what it actually guarded. — Tamsin doesn't answer, just checks her gear like she's leaving early.

topics.label: back Vell — the dead never held the pen
topics.say: Thank you. Precision matters, even in grief. — Lys looks at you like you've failed a much simpler test.

topics.label: tell them it's not yours to grade (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly the broken bargain isn't a fight for you to settle between them.
fx: "...An acceptable abstention." — Lys just nods once, already watching the road instead.
You'd let a debt collector off easy too, near as Lys is concerned. — Vell mutters something about the impossibility of pleasing hunters.

topics.label: leave it between them
topics.say: You tell Lys and Vell it's theirs to settle, and step back. They settle it the way people do: quietly, badly, and without you. Neither asks you again.

topics.label: back Vell — the crown is proof
topics.say: Thank you. Some things matter more than being comfortable to look at. — Lys just watches the road, unconvinced.

topics.label: that's enough — noted, and kept
topics.say: Do try not to lose anything important. I say that with more confidence in you than I expected to have.

topics.label: that's enough for now, carefully
topics.say: Do try not to lose anything important. I am keeping a closer count of you than I used to bother with.

topics.label: that's enough — this city keeps records
topics.say: Do try not to lose anything important here of all places. This city keeps better records than either of us.

topics.label: about what you just said
topics.say: "Mine," Vell says, not looking up from the hollow seat. "The first Reeve's line, exiled once it was inconvenient. I'm what's left of the quiet part." They wait on you to answer.

topics.label: press them on it
topics.say: You don't let them leave it there. "...I told myself the ledger was research," Vell says. "It wasn't. I needed to know if I came from a thief or from whoever he robbed. Both, it turns out."

topics.label: tell them it changes nothing between you
topics.say: "Blood or not," you say, "you're the same person you were an hour ago." Something in Vell's shoulders drops half an inch. "...Thank you," they say, like the word costs real effort.

topics.label: that's enough for now
topics.say: Do try not to lose anything important while I'm not looking.

topics.label: back Vell — the wreck deserves better
topics.say: Thank you. My own name's tangled up in that hull whether anyone credits it or not. — Lys just watches the water, unconvinced.

topics.label: back Vell — the record matters too
topics.say: Thank you. Rest doesn't require forgetting what rested there. — Osk looks like something in him has quietly closed.

topics.label: tell them it's not yours to grade (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly the drowned nave isn't a fight for you to settle between them.
fx: "...Fair. It was Fenmarch's grief before it was your footnote." — Vell, almost gracious: "Noted. I can wait."
Neither of you looks satisfied. — Vell taps the notebook shut, and doesn't open it again today.

topics.label: leave it between them
topics.say: You tell Brother Osk and Vell it's theirs to settle, and step back. They settle it the way people do: quietly, badly, and without you. Neither asks you again.

topics.label: back Vell — the barrows deserve better
topics.say: Thank you. Someone should mind what leaves that ground besides the grief. — Tamsin doesn't answer, just checks her gear like she's leaving early.

topics.label: call it a draw between them (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly the crown isn't yours to fight over between them.
fx: "...Fair. It was never mine to grieve or study for you." — Vell, after a moment: "Fair. Noted. Not forgotten."
Neither wanted that answer. — Lys watches the road; Vell writes something down without saying what.

topics.label: call it a draw between them (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly what's left of the Reeve's Pride isn't yours to fight over between them.
fx: "...Fair. It was never mine to grieve for you." — Vell, after a moment: "Fair. Noted. Not forgotten."
You'd let the wreckers vote on history too, near as Vell's concerned. — Lys just shrugs, still watching the water.

topics.label: call it a draw between them (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly the fort's founding isn't a fight for you to settle between them.
fx: "...Fine. Wasn't my lie to begin with." — Vell, almost gracious: "Nor mine to force on people still standing that wall."
You're as bad as a politician, near as Tamsin's concerned. — Vell says nothing, which from Vell is its own verdict.

topics.label: call it a draw between them (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly what leaves the barrows isn't a fight for you to settle between them.
fx: "...Fine. Wasn't my counter to police anyway." — Vell, almost gracious: "Nor mine to shut on people who need the coin."
Neither wanted that answer. — Tamsin goes back to her gear; Vell writes something down without saying what.

topics.label: call it a draw between them (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly the prior's confession isn't a fight for you to settle between them.
fx: "...That's fair. It should have been his choice from the start." — Vell, after a moment: "Fair. Noted. Not forgotten."
You go quiet in the way that means you mind. — Vell writes something down without saying what.

topics.label: back Vell — write every name down
topics.say: Thank you. A name written down is a name that outlives the ledger that once starved it. — Osk says nothing, just looks at the barn's doors a while longer.

topics.label: call the record a draw (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly whether the barn's dead get a record or a rite isn't yours to settle between them.
fx: "...Fair. The ledger was ours to answer for, not yours." — Vell, after a moment: "Fair. Noted. Not forgotten."
Neither wanted that answer. — Osk says a verse under his breath; Vell writes something down without saying what.

topics.label: leave it between them
topics.say: You tell Brother Osk and Vell it's theirs to settle, and step back. They settle it the way people do: quietly, badly, and without you. Neither asks you again.

topics.label: back Vell — showing up is honest enough
topics.say: Thank you. Showing up counts for more out here than anyone's paid to admit. — Tamsin only shakes her head, unconvinced.

topics.label: call the charter a draw (will)
topics.say: You tell them plainly whose coin bought the Shieldings' peace isn't yours to settle between them.
fx: "...Fair. It was the Watch's pride talking, not the field's." — Vell, after a moment: "Fair. Noted. Not forgotten."
Neither wanted that answer. — Tamsin goes back to counting the field's iron; Vell writes something down without saying what.

topics.label: leave it between them
topics.say: You tell Tamsin and Vell it's theirs to settle, and step back. They settle it the way people do: quietly, badly, and without you. Neither asks you again.

lys_whistle.name: a bone hunting-whistle
lys_whistle.hint: two low notes, and somewhere in the trees, she'll hear them.

osk_verse_scrap.name: a verse in an unsteady hand
osk_verse_scrap.hint: his own hand, mistakes and all — he wanted you to have it right, even wrong.

tamsin_hammer_charm.name: a thumbnail-small forge-charm
tamsin_hammer_charm.hint: her mother's iron. She doesn't explain further, and you don't ask.

vell_cipher_key.name: a strip of vellum, a cipher in hand
vell_cipher_key.hint: notes in Vell's own hand — might unlock more of theirs, if you find any.

stages.text: He's clear of debt, and staying with the Company anyway. That's his to choose, and he chose.
He's buried east of Camp Gallows, in Thornwold. Grief, not victory — but it's finished.
He's alive and found. What happens next in Thornwold isn't yours to force.
You're at Camp Gallows: in to the muster ground, west to the cook-fire, south to the scout line.
Ask after Lys's brother at Camp Gallows, in Thornwold west of the Vale — before Coldpass.
His family is found in the drowned nave. What happens next in Fenmarch isn't yours to force.
You're in Fenmarch. Ask after Osk's family at the drowned nave, near Reedholm.
Ask Osk about his family, then find Fenmarch east of the Vale — before Coldpass, or it stays as it is.
She's let the mine lie, in her own way. There's nothing more it can take from her now.
She knows the truth about the collapse. What she does with it in Cinderhall is hers to choose.
You're in the Iron Downs. Ask after the collapsed mine at Cinderhall.
Ask Tamsin about the mine, then find Cinderhall in the Iron Downs, past Thornwold — before Coldpass.
You're in Hollowbrook. Ask after the Keepers' Hall and the ledger it holds.
Vell goes quiet at the name Marrowgate. The Keepers' Hall in Hollowbrook might hold why.
Ask Vell about Marrowgate, then find the Keepers' Hall in Hollowbrook, north past Fenmarch — before Coldpass.

epilogue.text: Lys never got the chance to find her brother. Nobody else went looking either.
Lys walked out of your company on the road and never came back to it.
Lys brought her brother home to the Vale, and the hunter's camp is loud again, for the first time in years.
Lys buried her brother east of Camp Gallows and marked the spot the way hunters mark a trail.
Lys still watches the eastern road some evenings, though she's stopped saying why.
Lys stayed at the hunter's camp, watching the treeline, and never learned how the rest of it ended.
By the end Lys called you the steadiest thing on a road she never expected to walk this far down.
Lys still walks beside you, but she watches you now the way she watches strange ground — carefully, from a distance.
You told Lys to go to her brother herself, whatever it cost. She never forgot who said it first.
You called Cal a deserter once, in front of Lys. She went after him anyway, and never quite let it go.
Brother Osk's verse went unfinished. The chapel lit a candle and did not say why.
Brother Osk left your company on the road, verses and all, and did not send word after.
Brother Osk said the rite over his own family himself, and the Church quietly stopped calling him a novice.
Brother Osk has not quoted a verse since Fenmarch burned. He still wears the gray.
Brother Osk stayed in the chapel, tending a grief that was never quite his own to carry alone.
Brother Osk stopped calling himself a novice somewhere around you, though the Church never made it official.
Osk still says the rites when you ask him to, but he has stopped explaining them to you, and you have stopped asking why.
You told Osk his verses were worth saying. He has not stopped saying them since, badly, on purpose.
You called the old rites superstition, to Osk's face. He kept saying them anyway, just not to you.
Tamsin's hammer hangs unclaimed at the Vale forge. Nobody there swings it as hard.
Tamsin walked out of your company and didn't look back to see if you noticed.
Tamsin got her answer about the mine, and made whoever lied about it answer in turn.
Tamsin let the mine keep its dead in the end. She sounds tired more than angry now, when it comes up.
Tamsin has not spoken about the mine, or the miners, or much else, since Cinderhall sold them out.
Tamsin kept the Vale forge running and never went looking for what took her mother.
Tamsin swings her hammer easier with you at her back than she'd ever admit to the smith.
Tamsin still marches with you, but she counts your blows now the way she counts an enemy's, out of old habit.
You told Tamsin to make them answer for the mine. She did, and never asked if you approved.
You called her mother's death wasted iron, once. Tamsin still swings a hammer. She just swings it alone.
Vell's last sentence went unfinished, and nobody who heard it start ever learned how it ended.
Vell left your company somewhere on the road, taking their notes and their silences with them.
Vell found the Keepers' ledger, and whatever it says about their birth, they carry it quietly now, on their own terms.
Vell's lineage came out before they were ready, dragged into daylight by someone else's hand. They have not forgiven it.
Vell stayed at the Last Light inn, still evasive about Marrowgate, and never did explain why.
Vell stopped being careful with you somewhere along the road, and started being honest instead.
Vell still travels with you, notebook closed more often than open now, and asks you fewer questions than before.
You told Vell the truth was worth knowing, whatever it cost them. They paid it, and kept walking.
You told Vell to burn the ledger and be done. They didn't. They still wonder if you were right.
You swore to keep Vell's name out of it, then sold it for gold and standing. Vell hasn't forgiven that.
You kept Vell's name out of it, as you swore; they never learned how close it came.
You never swore to protect Vell's name. You kept it quiet anyway, and never mentioned that either.
Lys walked with you to the end with her brother's name still unspoken; the road to Camp Gallows is still there, and she still means it.
Brother Osk never reached the drowned nave with you. He says the verses for his family anyway, over water that isn't theirs.
Tamsin never got to Cinderhall with you. The mine keeps its answer, and she keeps swinging at whatever is nearest.
Tamsin has her answer about the mine now. She has not told you, or herself, what she means to do with it.
Vell's ledger stayed unread in Hollowbrook's Keepers' Hall. They walked with you to the end still not saying what Marrowgate means to them.
Vell's ledger stayed unread in the Keepers' Hall. They told you what Marrowgate means to them anyway, and walked with you to the end.
Lys went down once on the road with you, and got up. She tells it as a joke, and watches your face while she does.
Brother Osk was carried clear of a fight once, and says the rite for it every year, half in thanks and half in complaint.
Tamsin still keeps the dent in her pauldron from the blow that put her down beside you. She won't have it hammered out.
Vell went down once with you and wrote up the whole affair afterwards, leaving out only the part where they screamed.
Lys and Brother Osk still walk together, unlikely as it once looked — a hunter's quiet keeping pace with a novice's verses.
Lys never wavered on you. Brother Osk stopped explaining his doubts to her, and she stopped asking him to.
Lys and Tamsin talk less than either would admit, and still know exactly when to guard each other's backs.
Tamsin still swears by you. Lys stopped arguing the point with her on the road, and started watching quietly instead.
Lys still doesn't trust a man who won't say where he's from. Vell still doesn't trust anyone. They manage anyway.
Lys kept faith in you to the end. Vell kept a careful distance from both of you, and wrote none of it down.
Brother Osk still says a verse before Tamsin swings her hammer. She still says it doesn't help. Neither one stops.
Tamsin backed you without blinking. Brother Osk kept walking beside you anyway, quieter than he used to be.
Brother Osk got Vell to sit through a whole verse without interrupting it. Vell has still not admitted he liked it.
Osk never stopped trusting you, plainly and out loud. Vell never quite matched it, and never explained why.
Tamsin re-tempers Vell's pens now the way she tempers blades, and swears she doesn't know why she bothers. She knows.
Tamsin never asked Vell to justify their caution about you. She just started standing a little closer, just in case.
You told Osk the roll-book doesn't drown a boy twice. He never fully argued the point again, or forgave it either.
You backed Osk's Priory over Lys's anger at the sexton's roll. She still thinks of that boy, some nights.
You told Lys and Osk the sexton's roll wasn't yours to fight over. They let it go between them, mostly.
Lys and Osk never settled it, over one drowned boy's name. It sits between them still, unspoken.
You told Tamsin the rite still mattered, fire or no fire. Osk kept his verses. Tamsin kept her opinion of them.
You told Osk to let the fire decide, twice over. He still says a verse for every one he couldn't stop.
You told Osk and Tamsin the fire wasn't theirs to fight over between them. Neither much liked the answer, and both kept it.
Osk and Tamsin never settled it, rite against fire. They still work the same road, and still don't talk about it.

You backed Tamsin's hard line at the glade. The rope went back up, and Lys never quite forgave the arithmetic of it.
You told Lys and Tamsin the glade's rope wasn't yours to settle between them. They dropped it, mostly, and moved on.

You told Osk and Vell the prior's confession wasn't theirs to fight over. They left it there, mostly settled.

You told Tamsin and Vell the fort's lie wasn't theirs to fight over. They dropped it, and the wall stands the same as before.
Tamsin and Vell never settled it, the Watch's honor against the truth of it. They still work the same roads, carefully apart.

You backed Osk on the barrow doors, left open for grief's sake. Tamsin still checks that hill more than she says.
You backed Osk against sealing the barrow, though sealed it stayed. He still says a verse at the stone, some days.
You backed Tamsin on the barrow doors, sealed for the living's sake. Osk still says a verse at the stone, some days.

You told Lys and Vell the crown wasn't theirs to fight over between them. They let it go, mostly, and moved on.
